The viewer scheduler and snapshot capture provide their own off-STA execution. Direct callers needing responsiveness must choose an appropriate execution thread. Operation and owned-resource cleanup failures are preserved together, with the operation failure first. Region ownership is handed to the caller only after source lease cleanup succeeds; an undeliverable region is disposed by the operation. Pixel and statistics results carry the queried lease's FrameInfo. PixelSamplesResult and RegionStatistics copy constructor inputs and expose read-only collections that can be retained and shared. Pixel providers transfer their returned sample arrays to the caller and must not reuse or mutate them after returning. FrameLease.Info.Descriptor always describes its own pixels. Unsubmitted frames, including derived pixel buffers, have FrameId 0 and no source timestamp. Submission assigns a viewer-local ID to the submitted lease; leases acquired before submission remain unsubmitted. RegionPixels.SourceFrame and ImageSnapshot.SourceFrame identify their input frame. Their Region is expressed in that input frame's coordinates. AcquirePixels() returns an independent lease describing the cropped or converted pixels, without copying source metadata onto it. Queries on that lease use local coordinates and describe the derived pixels; retain the containing region/snapshot when source provenance is needed. RegionPixels owns its independent CPU image and must be disposed. It is created by FrameLease.ReadRegionAsync after validating the provider result; consumers cannot construct it directly. Unsupported capabilities fail without download fallback. CPU formats remain Gray8/Gray16/Gray32Float/Rgb24/Bgr24/Bgr32/Bgra32/Pbgra32/Rgba32. Statistics return count/min/max/mean per semantic channel (Gray or R/G/B[/A]); non-finite floating values are ignored, with zero count and null statistics when no finite values exist. Premultiplied channels stay premultiplied. RegionStatistics.Channels uses Gray, R/G/B or R/G/B/A order regardless of source byte order; Bgr32 padding is excluded. Construction rejects unknown formats and incorrect channel counts. External IFramePixelSource implementations must follow that ordering and return the source frame's format; frame leases reject a mismatched format. Display ranges do not constrain original query values, including Gray32Float values outside the default 0–1 display range. One pixel query scheduler per viewer captures geometry on STA and queries off STA, with at most one batch in flight. Each batch executes and publishes either one ROI or a shared gather for due mouse and line coordinates. Oldest-due selection serves pending work fairly; unselected requests retain no frame lease and capture fresh geometry/frame on a later tick. Slow ROI queries therefore do not age one another or delay publication of a completed gather. Point and line coordinates use the half-open pixel coverage rectangle [0, Width) × [0, Height): pixel (x, y) covers [x, x+1) × [y, y+1). Lines are clipped to that coverage, their endpoints are floored to pixel indices, and Bresenham samples retain the input direction and both endpoint pixels. Very large finite coordinates use exact clipping of the supplied binary values to avoid losing the pixel interval; this cannot recover precision already lost before calling the API. A crossing endpoint on the outer right/bottom boundary is clamped to the last covered pixel; a line lying on or only touching those exclusive edges has no samples. ROI geometry uses floor(left/top), ceil(right/bottom), then image intersection; empty regions are not queried. Shape editors preserve statistics labels. The separate interaction coordinator manages selection, editing and creation sessions. See measurement ownership and interaction for geometry and extension contracts. Viewer.QueryOptions accepts PixelQueryOptions: PixelQueryRateHz=30, LineQueryRateHz=30, RegionQueryRateHz=10 Hz, MaxResultAge=100 ms, all positive. Each rate must produce a representable interval of at least one TimeSpan tick and less than TimeSpan.MaxValue; invalid settings are rejected when assigned. Due requests are served in due order; pending geometry is replaced by its latest state without resetting the execution interval, including during edits and resizes. Monotonic age starts at the frame/geometry snapshot, not camera capture time. Geometry changes, deletion, disabling and closing invalidate old work. Results may describe a recent prior frame within the age limit; advancing video clears expired values, while an unchanged paused frame keeps its valid result. FrameId stays in API results/logging and is never a HUD label. QueryMetrics.Batches counts completed backend batches, including batches containing failed queries; it is not a successful-query or publication count. ExpiredResults counts individual completed results rejected at publication for exceeding MaxResultAge, not already displayed values later cleared by a scheduler tick. LastDurationMilliseconds spans frame/geometry capture through backend completion, including worker scheduling but excluding the wait for STA publication and its callbacks. The bottom-left pixel HUD has its own cap of min(10, PixelQueryRateHz) Hz, with a full interval after each completed query (including failures). Mouse moves coalesce to the latest target without resetting that interval. It may publish a recently sampled position from the same interaction session; the coordinates and value always update together. Other measurements still require the exact geometry version. While waiting, the HUD retains the complete previous result for up to 300 ms from its sampling start if the target or frame has changed, then shows —. An unchanged static result does not expire. Failures show — immediately; MaxResultAge still controls whether a newly completed query can publish. Leaving the image, disabling the HUD or losing the frame hides it and prevents old work from reappearing. The non-interactive HUD has no background and uses invariant numeric formatting with a minimum of seven characters per value. Longer values remain complete; narrow viewports clip the HUD rather than wrapping or resizing. Each target capture recomputes the image coordinate from the current container pointer and viewport transform, including when fit, layout or image dimensions change without mouse movement. Hidden/unloaded viewports and pointers outside the container have no query target. Freeze, snapshot and save Opening the context menu freezes the current frame, clears pending input and invalidates in-flight pre-freeze submissions. Closing it resumes new input. A menu-scoped lease pins the frame and display settings through Click/Closed ordering; saving acquires its own lease before the file dialog. The menu lease is released when input drains or on viewer shutdown. Capture, encoding and ownership contracts are in snapshots. Export retains the committed mapping, never an uncommitted display-range request. Shutdown and integrations Stop and await the producer before awaiting Viewer disposal; never block the Viewer STA. Admitted submissions drain through final release and public result completion, including replacement cleanup on submitting threads. Independent leases can outlive the Viewer. See Viewer shutdown for the shared completion and failure contract. Application adapters convert their own images to ImageFrame. Use Copy for borrowed CPU storage, TakeOwnership for immutable owned storage, and D3D9ImageFrame.TakeOwnership for ready GPU surfaces. Conversion, device compatibility and adapter tests belong to the consumer. Submit GPU frames GPU frames use the same ImageFrame submission API. They require producer integration; a CPU array or arbitrary native pointer is not a GPU frame. Ready D3D9 surface This adapter accepts resources already created and synchronized by the producer: static ValueTask<FrameSubmitResult> SubmitSurfaceAsync( Viewer viewer, FrameDescriptor originalDescriptor, nint readySurface, IFramePixelSource originalPixels, Action releaseResources) { var frame = D3D9ImageFrame.TakeOwnership( originalDescriptor, readySurface, originalPixels, releaseResources); return viewer.SubmitFrameAsync(frame); } Supply a WPF-compatible, non-multisampled IDirect3DSurface9 render target in D3DPOOL_DEFAULT, using premultiplied D3DFMT_A8R8G8B8 pixels. Finish GPU writes and release compute mappings before transfer. The descriptor and IFramePixelSource describe original pixels; the surface must match their standard display conversion. Keep the device, surface and query resources valid and immutable until releaseResources runs. Ownership transfers even on factory failure. See the GPU contract before implementing an adapter. GPU surfaces and explicit pixel queries D3D9ImageFrame.TakeOwnership(descriptor, surface, pixelSource, release) transfers a ready, immutable BGRA IDirect3DSurface9 and its producer-owned lifetime. The producer must supply matching dimensions, a WPF-compatible D3D9 render target, and raw pixels consistent with the standard display conversion. The surface cannot be overwritten while any lease exists. The external-surface entry is a trusted native boundary: a nonzero pointer is not proof of compatibility. Supply a valid, non-multisampled D3DFMT_A8R8G8B8 render target in D3DPOOL_DEFAULT, with premultiplied alpha and dimensions matching the descriptor. Use a WPF-compatible device (the provided CUDA component uses D3D9Ex with D3DCREATE_MULTITHREADED and D3DCREATE_FPU_PRESERVE). The producer owns device compatibility, native metadata validation and GPU synchronization. Finish all writes and relinquish compute mappings before transfer; merely enqueueing GPU work is insufficient. Keep the device, surface and original query resources valid until the final release callback. The descriptor describes original pixels, not the BGRA surface's byte layout. No custom color mapping, orientation change or display range is represented by this API; Display snapshots reconstruct the standard display conversion from original pixels rather than reading the surface. GPU submissions share the same latest-frame scheduler, FrameId, freeze/cancellation semantics and commit callbacks. D3DImage is created and bound on the viewer STA; no DisplayConverter or CPU pixel provider is invoked on the normal GPU display path. Front-buffer restoration rebinds the retained current surface. CPU submissions switch back to WriteableBitmap. IFramePixelSource supplies asynchronous gather, statistics and region reads independently of the display surface. The library has no CUDA dependency. The producer retains its source image and query resources until the final frame lease is released. Query failures affect interaction, not display, and must never trigger an implicit full-image readback. Cancellation of submitted GPU work must retain buffers and leases until device completion, even when publication is cancelled. Region reads transfer an independently owned CPU ImageFrame with the requested dimensions and source format. Coordinates in that image start at the region's origin; FrameLease adds source provenance in RegionPixels. A provider must finish access to source resources before its operation returns or throws, including cancellation. The frame's release callback owns the provider's resources; the library does not separately dispose the provider. This completion rule applies to every provider method. Independent leases, direct reads, the query scheduler and snapshot capture can call the same provider concurrently, including different methods. The provider must support that concurrency or serialize its own backend access. The scheduler's single batch and the export gate do not serialize all provider calls. DisplayRange is unsupported for GPU surfaces; producers must apply their GPU mapping before submission. Consumers are responsible for converting source formats to the supported frame contract. Surface loss due to a driver reset is distinct from WPF front-buffer availability and is not recovered by recreating the producer's device here. No software rendering fallback is enabled. If a WPF front-buffer restoration callback fails, the presenter stops accepting GPU surfaces. The presentation owner retains that error for Viewer.DisposeAsync(), including after switching to CPU display; it does not throw the error out of the WPF event callback or retry restoration. This asynchronous failure does not change a previously returned submission result. If surface attachment fails, presentation stops using that presenter. A successful detach permits lease release; if detachment cannot be confirmed, the presenter and potentially attached leases are retained for process lifetime. This deliberate isolation prevents native use after release and is reported as a failure, not automatic recovery. The optional CUDA component supplies native display conversion and original-pixel queries for Gray8/Bgr24/Rgb24/Bgra32/Pbgra32/Rgba32. Application adapters still supply their source-frame and runtime integration; the WPF assembly itself has no CUDA dependency.

docs/en/getting-started.html.title: Getting started | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started 简体中文 Build a small application that displays an image, then choose a component guide for your next task. Create a viewer Use Windows and .NET 8 with a net8.0-windows project and <UseWPF>true</UseWPF>. Create a console project with this project file, then install the package: <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk"> <PropertyGroup> <OutputType>Exe</OutputType> <TargetFramework>net8.0-windows</TargetFramework> <UseWPF>true</UseWPF> <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings> <Nullable>enable</Nullable> </PropertyGroup> </Project> dotnet add package Fizzy.ImageViewer Viewer creates its own STA; a console application can use it without creating an application dispatcher. With implicit usings enabled, this is a complete console entry point: using Fizzy.ImageViewer; using Fizzy.ImageViewer.Frames; await using var viewer = new Viewer(showWindow: false); var closed = new TaskCompletionSource( TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously); viewer.Closed += (_, _) => closed.TrySetResult(); viewer.Title = "My first image"; var pixels = new byte[640 * 480]; Array.Fill(pixels, (byte)128); var result = await viewer.SubmitFrameAsync(ImageFrame.Copy( new FrameDescriptor(640, 480, 640, FramePixelFormat.Gray8), pixels)); if (result.Error is { } error) throw error; if (result.Status != FrameSubmitStatus.Committed) throw new InvalidOperationException($"Initial frame: {result.Status}"); viewer.Show(); await closed.Task; // await using waits for shutdown and reports cleanup failures. Configure and subscribe before Show(). Submission transfers ownership immediately, even when cancelled or closed: do not submit the same frame twice or dispose its transferred storage. Committed means the UI accepted the frame, not that the monitor has displayed it. Inspect both Status and Error, including for dropped frames. Closed is a notification, not proof that rendering and queries have drained. Stop and await your producer before awaiting DisposeAsync; never synchronously wait for either from a Viewer callback. A Viewer has one window lifetime; create a new instance after closure. Basic operations Use the wheel to zoom and the middle button to pan. The context menu offers measurements and image export. To add features programmatically, place these calls before viewer.Show() in the example: viewer.HudLabelText = "My image"; viewer.IsPixelInfoEnabled = true; viewer.ActivateMeasurementTool( Fizzy.ImageViewer.Measurements.MeasurementToolIds.Length); Click two points to measure a length in image pixels. Escape ends creation or editing. See measurements to observe results, drawing to add annotations, and snapshots to save image pixels. Complete examples Run from the repository root. These manual checks open WPF windows: dotnet run --project samples/BasicViewer dotnet run --project samples/LiveOverlays dotnet run --project samples/MeasurementsAndExport BasicViewer: copied grayscale pixels and awaited closure. LiveOverlays: simulated frames, reusable batch handle, production ending before disposal. MeasurementsAndExport: fresh-session point tool, events and PNG output under artifacts/samples/. ./scripts/Test-Samples.ps1 builds without opening windows. Export accepts an optional output directory; choose one without a valuable existing snapshot.png. Advanced integration Continue with CPU/GPU frames, CUDA integration, or live-streaming ownership and performance.

docs/en/live-streaming.html.title: Live streaming | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/live-streaming.html.summary: Live streaming 简体中文 Integrate a camera or other continuous producer after completing Getting started. The viewer bounds its own frame queue; your application owns acquisition, upstream buffering, overlay scheduling, and producer shutdown. Start with LiveOverlays, a simulated producer that reuses drawing handles and stops before viewer disposal. Bound work before submission The viewer processes one submission and retains only the newest waiting frame. Replaced waiting frames complete as Superseded; it is a live display, not a lossless recording queue. For a pull-based producer, await each submission before producing the next frame, as in LiveOverlays. This limits producer work naturally. For a push camera callback, keep an application-owned bounded latest-frame handoff and a worker that observes every submission result. Release any owned frame discarded before submission. Avoid a growing Task.Run queue, unbounded channel or list of submission tasks: the viewer's queue cannot bound work allocated upstream. Stop admission and drain the producer during shutdown. Awaiting a submission observes commit/drop and any release error for that submission; it does not mean the camera buffer is reusable. Only the final release callback establishes that for transferred storage. Track status counts and errors without logging every successful frame in a hot callback. Live camera overlays: consumer requirements Keep layers and batches alive for the display session. A camera frame is a data update, not a reason to recreate the visual tree. Consumers of continuous camera or detection streams must follow these rules: Avoid in the frame loop Use instead Clear() followed by Add(...), or disposing and recreating batches Create each batch once and call Replace(...) on it Calling DrawCircle, DrawLine, etc. once per detection Submit the complete detection collection in one batch per independently managed group Posting a dispatcher callback or starting a task for every incoming result Keep one latest pending result and consume it from one serialized, rate-limited display loop Repainting fixed ROI, crosshairs, and labels with every camera frame Keep static content in separate batches; update only changed content Creating mutable brushes for every element or frame Reuse frozen brushes, such as Brushes.Lime Recreating HUD handles on every status update Keep the handle and call Update only when content changes For example, the following operations belong to three different lifecycle stages; do not put the initialization or cleanup in the per-frame callback: using Fizzy.ImageViewer.Drawing; using System.Windows; using System.Windows.Media; // Initialization: retain these handles for the display session. var detections = viewer.Layers.CreateDrawingLayer("camera-detections"); var batch = detections.Add(Array.Empty<DrawingElement>()); // Display update: call from ONE serialized consumer at the chosen display rate. // Build this collection only for the latest result selected for display. batch.Replace(new DrawingElement[] { new CircleElement(new Point(100, 100), 8, Brushes.Lime, 2), new RectangleElement(new Rect(20, 20, 50, 40), Brushes.Yellow) }); // A valid result with no detections clears content while retaining the visual. batch.Replace(Array.Empty<DrawingElement>()); // Shutdown: first stop and await the producer/display loop, then release handles. batch.Dispose(); viewer.Layers.RemoveLayer(detections); Choose the display rate independently of acquisition/inference (for example, 30 or 60 updates per second, subject to measured rendering cost). Overwrite stale pending results rather than queueing them. No new result means no Replace call; a new empty result means Replace(Array.Empty<DrawingElement>()). Build drawing elements after selecting the latest result so discarded results do not allocate unused drawing objects. Release overwritten results if they own pooled buffers or other resources, and do not mutate a result while the display consumer reads it. Replace is synchronous and marshals visual work to the viewer thread. It does not throttle, merge, or drop updates. The image pipeline's latest-frame queue does not apply to overlay calls, and image submission plus overlay replacement is not an atomic, frame-synchronized presentation. Consumers needing matching image and detection results must track frame identity and define their own stale-result policy. Do not hold a producer lock while calling viewer APIs. Replace reuses the visual, not all drawing allocations: submission copies the collection, shares immutable elements whose brushes are already frozen, and clones elements/brushes when mutable brushes require a snapshot. Each update records commands directly into the existing visual, avoiding intermediate DrawingGroup and per-primitive geometry objects. WPF command buffers and resource references still allocate. Equal pen styles share frozen pens within one preparation using a bounded cache; text formatting still allocates. Reusing the input array alone does not remove these allocations. Frozen brushes avoid brush cloning, but do not make replacement allocation-free. Batching reduces visual count; it is not a guarantee of zero GC or a particular frame rate. Clear, layer removal, and viewer closure invalidate batch handles. If the host allows Clear All Shapes during streaming, serialize that action with the display loop and recreate the batch once before resuming; do not retry a disposed handle on every frame. Stop subscriptions/timers and await in-flight updates before teardown. Do not call GC.Collect() in the frame loop. Measure allocation, GC counts and update latency with the expected marker count and zoom behavior; see benchmark scope. Reduce copies and conversion Keep the source's supported format and stride. Do not expand Gray8 to BGRA or reorder RGB/BGR solely for display. Native 8-bit CPU layouts are preserved where supported; Gray16, Gray32Float, Rgba32 and remapped Gray8 require display conversion. Reuse a producer buffer with Copy, or transfer a separately owned immutable buffer with TakeOwnership. Copy already rents internal memory; add producer pooling only after measuring allocations and retention. Never refill transferred memory early. Reuse one Viewer for the window lifetime. Stable image dimensions and display format allow its two CPU WriteableBitmaps to be reused. Change display range when needed, rather than requesting a redraw every frame. For pixels already on the GPU, use a supported GPU adapter to avoid a full-image round trip. GPU integration is not automatically faster for CPU input and still has allocation, synchronization and copy costs. Limit query work Pixel inspection, profiles and region statistics need not run at camera frame rate. For example, configure lighter query limits before showing the viewer: viewer.QueryOptions = new Fizzy.ImageViewer.Imaging.PixelQueryOptions { PixelQueryRateHz = 15, LineQueryRateHz = 10, RegionQueryRateHz = 5, MaxResultAge = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200) }; These are application choices, not performance guarantees. The viewer shares one query batch at a time; the pixel HUD also caps itself at 10 Hz. MaxResultAge controls stale-result acceptance, not how quickly a query executes. Use QueryMetrics to inspect duration and expired results. Prefer point/ROI requests over full snapshots, especially for GPU sources. Dispose owned leases, regions and snapshots promptly; they retain memory and may extend a camera buffer's lifetime. Direct CPU query methods can run synchronously on the caller, so move expensive analysis off the UI thread. Keep callbacks short and measure the whole path OnCommitted and FrameCommitted run on the Viewer STA. Do not perform encoding, device waits, heavy analysis, synchronous task waits or a submission-and-wait inside them. For asynchronous work, acquire an independent lease before the callback returns and release it when work finishes; the callback's borrowed lease cannot be retained as-is. Bound this background work too. Measure producer conversion/copy cost, managed allocation, submission status counts, query duration and overlay update cost separately. Submission completion is not physical presentation latency. Run the frame, drawing and query benchmarks for the path you change, then validate interaction and display on the target machine. Synthetic benchmarks do not establish sustained camera throughput or mixed-DPI behavior.

docs/en/measurement-tools.html.title: Custom measurement tools | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/measurement-tools.html.summary: Custom measurement tools 简体中文 Implement a tool when an application needs its own interactive creation workflow. Start with built-in measurements if the existing tools are sufficient. Noninteractive annotations use drawing layers; there is no standalone measurement creation or saved-ROI restoration API. Create and register a tool This complete tool creates a rectangle with the same editing, statistics and notifications as the built-in ROI. Each activation gets a new session. using Fizzy.ImageViewer.Measurements; using System.Windows; public sealed class CustomRoi : IMeasurementTool { public string Id => "custom-roi"; public string DisplayName => "Custom ROI"; public IMeasurementToolSession CreateSession(IMeasurementToolContext context) => new Session(context); private sealed class Session(IMeasurementToolContext context) : IMeasurementToolSession { private IMeasurement? _preview; private Point _start; public MeasurementClickResult OnClick(Point point) { if (_preview is null or { IsDisposed: true }) { _start = point; _preview = context.CreateMeasurement( MeasurementGeometry.Rectangle(point, point), new() { Query = MeasurementQueryKind.RegionStatistics }); return MeasurementClickResult.Continue; } OnMouseMove(point); _preview.Complete(); return MeasurementClickResult.Finish; } public void OnMouseMove(Point point) { if (_preview is { IsDisposed: false }) _preview.UpdateGeometry(MeasurementGeometry.Rectangle(_start, point)); } // The framework releases unfinished measurements after cancellation. public void Cancel() { } public void Dispose() { } } } Keep the registration alive while the feature is installed: using var registration = viewer.RegisterMeasurementTool(new CustomRoi()); viewer.ActivateMeasurementTool("custom-roi"); Choose a query using the geometry/query table. Call Complete() for every item that should survive the session; returning Finish only ends input. Tool registration ownership RegisterMeasurementTool(tool) returns an IDisposable handle for that registration. Dispose it from any thread to revoke only that instance and cancel its active session. Disposal is idempotent and safe after viewer closure; completed measurements survive. The caller owns the tool object, which is never disposed by the registration. Keep the handle for the installing component's lifetime. Ignoring it retains the registration until global unregistration or viewer closure. Registration captures Id and DisplayName once on the Viewer STA. After those external getters return, the viewer checks its lifetime again before accepting the registration. If a getter closes the viewer reentrantly, registration is rejected with ObjectDisposedException and no tool is retained. UnregisterMeasurementTool(id) is a viewer-wide management operation: it removes whichever registration currently has that ID. Component cleanup should instead dispose its own handle, so it cannot remove a replacement registered under the same ID. Revocation takes effect before cancellation callbacks. Callback failures propagate to explicit callers after cleanup; they do not restore the revoked registration. Activation captures the registration instance before interrupting the previous session. Invalid initial requests preserve the current interaction. Reentrant callbacks may supersede a request; the superseded request never activates a same-ID replacement. Built-in menu actions retain the registration captured when the menu opens and ignore it if revoked, hidden, input-disabled or clearing when clicked. Extension boundary Measurement tools use a stable, ordinal Id for programmatic lookup and a separate DisplayName for menus. Registration rejects duplicate IDs; UnregisterMeasurementTool removes only the registry entry and cancels an active session for that ID while leaving completed measurement items intact. Menus are backed by the same registry and are updated for subsequent openings when tools are registered or unregistered. Use viewer.ActivateMeasurementTool(MeasurementToolIds.Length) for built-in tools; the other constants are Point, RectangleRoi and LineProfile. Custom tools implement both Id and DisplayName, and are installed with RegisterMeasurementTool. IDs are case-sensitive; blank IDs or display names are rejected. ActivateMeasurementTool throws KeyNotFoundException for an unknown ID and InvalidOperationException when the measurement layer is hidden or its configured hit testing is disabled. UnregisterMeasurementTool(id) returns whether an entry was removed. Call EndInteraction() to cancel creation or end editing; completed measurements and applied edits remain. Built-in and custom registrations implement IMeasurementTool: Id, DisplayName, and CreateSession(IMeasurementToolContext). Each activation calls the factory on the viewer STA and requires a new IMeasurementToolSession. Store preview handles, first-click coordinates and other mutable interaction state in this session. The registration contains reusable configuration; sharing it across viewers requires a thread-safe factory and configuration. The session receives OnClick(Point), OnMouseMove(Point) and Cancel() callbacks and retains its own creation context. Returning MeasurementClickResult.Finish from OnClick ends input; Continue retains it; call Complete() on each measurement to retain it. Unfinished measurements are released automatically. Normal completion does not call Cancel; interruption calls it once after ending the creation context and releases previews even if cancellation throws. Every returned session is disposed exactly once on the STA, including normal completion, callback failure and factory supersession. Put session-only resource cleanup in Dispose; keep Cancel for cancellation-specific behavior. The creation context ends before either callback. A disposal callback can start a replacement during normal operation; the old session's cleanup cannot end that replacement. Factories may create previews and may reenter viewer APIs. A newer activation takes precedence. If a factory returns after its activation was interrupted, its returned session is cancelled without changing the newer session. A factory failure or null return releases its unfinished measurements; the factory owns cleanup of resources not yet transferred to a measurement. A retained context cannot create measurements after its activation ends. For asynchronous work, call context.Finish() to end only that context's activation after committing the items to retain. It dispatches to the viewer STA and returns false for an ended, superseded or closed context; it never ends a replacement session. IMeasurement.Complete() commits one item and releases its reference to the creation context without finishing the tool session. Each context, item and event snapshot retains Origin with the registration's ToolId and activation's SessionId; multiple items from one activation share the origin, while later activations get a new session ID. Revoking a registration during cancellation invalidates an outer request to start that registration, even when another registration subsequently uses the same ID. Reentry, cancellation and failure During normal operation, a session started synchronously inside a tool callback or completion notification takes precedence, even when it uses the same tool. Returning or throwing from the old callback does not cancel that session or restore its input state. This also applies when cancellation interrupts an outer start request: the callback's session wins. Exceptions from tool callbacks propagate to explicit API callers; framework input and plot-window callbacks log failures and keep the viewer usable. Cleanup restores idle only if that operation still owns the session. When operation and cleanup both fail, an aggregate retains the original failure first and the cleanup failure after it; cleanup still attempts all owned resources. Completion/removal notification subscribers are instead isolated: their exceptions are logged and later subscribers still run. Cancellation ends the outgoing creation context before invoking the tool and then releases that session's unfinished items. Normal completion also ends the context and releases only its unfinished items. Completed items belong to the measurement collection until removal. A callback interrupted by a newer session cannot create through its old context; creation throws ObjectDisposedException. Measurements created by the new session survive cleanup, even when a disposal callback starts it. Cleanup attempts every owned preview and propagates combined session and preview failures to explicit callers. Framework input callbacks log these failures; viewer shutdown includes them in DisposeAsync. Bulk measurement cleanup rejects new measurement creation. Once viewer shutdown begins, ActivateMeasurementTool throws ObjectDisposedException; shutdown cleans both completed and unfinished measurements and waits for owned queries. Resources and threads Tool callbacks, context creation and notifications run on the viewer STA. Returned IMeasurement handles dispatch reads, updates and subscription changes to that STA, so background work can update or complete a live preview without retaining a dispatcher. Cancellation still disposes unfinished previews; late updates/completion then throw ObjectDisposedException. The handle supplied by MeasurementEventArgs.Measurement also supports application-driven updates to completed measurements. Dispose and event unsubscription are safe after closure; Id, Origin and IsDisposed remain readable, while other access requires a running viewer. Do not block STA callbacks waiting for workers that call these handles. Use AddResource and OnDispose to bind external resources and event subscriptions to the measurement. AddResource transfers ownership only when it succeeds. If it throws, the call does not change ownership: a new resource remains the caller's responsibility, while re-registering the same instance is rejected and leaves the measurement's existing ownership intact. Do not share an owned resource across measurements. Unregistering a tool retains completed measurements. Selection and deletion target the measurement owner, which removes both its primary visual and label. Setting Measurements.IsVisible = false cancels previews but retains completed items. Viewer.Hide() retains the active tool session and previews; clear and viewer closure dispose all items. Disposal revokes queries, executes cleanup callbacks, disposes resources, closes the plot and removes visuals. Every stage is attempted after failures. Explicit disposal aggregates cleanup errors. Explicit layer clearing and interaction cancellation propagate cleanup errors after attempting all items; framework input callbacks log them. Viewer shutdown includes resource cleanup failures in its shared DisposeAsync result. Disposal is idempotent and does not retry resources whose disposal already ran. Creation is rejected during bulk cleanup and shutdown. Geometry/result and viewer event subscriber failures are logged and isolated. Viewer.FrameCommitted is a viewer-level notification, not a query execution callback. See measurement results and Viewer lifetime.

docs/en/measurements.html.title: Measurements and interaction | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/measurements.html.summary: Measurements and interaction 简体中文 Use built-in tools to measure points, lengths, rectangular regions and line profiles. Positions and lengths use image pixels; noninteractive annotations belong in drawing layers. Activate a built-in tool The snippets assume a live viewer from Getting started. using Fizzy.ImageViewer.Measurements; viewer.ActivateMeasurementTool(MeasurementToolIds.Length); Tool ID Interaction Result Point Click a point Pixel value Length Click two endpoints Length in image pixels RectangleRoi Click opposite corners Region statistics LineProfile Click two endpoints Pixel samples and a profile window Use the context menu to choose a tool, or activate its ID. Unknown IDs throw KeyNotFoundException; a hidden or input-disabled measurement layer rejects activation with InvalidOperationException. Activation after shutdown starts throws ObjectDisposedException. Observing built-in and custom measurements Use Viewer.MeasurementChanged (also on IViewer) to observe completed items without implementing a tool or accessing WPF visuals. Geometry edits, query publication and result invalidation all carry the measurement ID, immutable geometry/version and current immutable QueryResult. QueryResult is null after geometry changes, query failure or expiration. Previews do not emit this event, and an unchanged geometry or already-empty result does not emit it. viewer.MeasurementChanged += (_, e) => { var id = e.Snapshot.Id; var geometry = e.Snapshot.Geometry; var result = e.QueryResult; // Null means the measurement currently has no valid pixel result. // Retain these immutable values or dispatch them to the application's UI. }; viewer.ActivateMeasurementTool(MeasurementToolIds.RectangleRoi); Viewer and handle notifications share one FIFO queue on the viewer STA. Each mutation captures immutable payloads and its subscribers before delivery; reentrant mutations append their events after the current mutation's notifications. Every subscriber sees nondecreasing geometry versions, completion precedes removal, and removal is terminal. The live handle may already reflect a later mutation or disposal while an older snapshot is delivered. Closing from a subscriber preserves queued measurement events and emits Closed after removals. Subscriber exceptions are logged and isolated. The event's Measurement can be disposed from any thread, including reentrantly from a callback. Completion and removal events carry the same result snapshot field, but completion does not promise query readiness. Custom tools may additionally subscribe to IMeasurement.GeometryChanged and QueryResultChanged on their own items. Edit and remove Click a completed measurement to edit it, and drag its control points. Delete removes the selected item; Escape ends creation or editing and retains already-applied edits. Use the event's Measurement handle for programmatic UpdateGeometry or Dispose, and viewer.Measurements.Clear() to remove all measurements. Geometry, editing and notifications Create geometry with MeasurementGeometry.Point, Crosshair, Line, Rectangle or Circle. Point and crosshair use Position; lines use Start/End; rectangles normalize opposite corners. Circles use Center and Radius. Factories return the sealed concrete records PointMeasurementGeometry, CrosshairMeasurementGeometry, LineMeasurementGeometry, RectangleMeasurementGeometry and CircleMeasurementGeometry. Pattern-match these types when reading a handle or event snapshot; unsupported coordinate properties do not exist. Kinds use the measurement-specific MeasurementGeometryKind enum. Bounds returns normalized image-space bounds: endpoint bounds for lines and rectangles, diameter bounds for circles, and zero extent for points and crosshairs. Line endpoints retain their original order. Coordinates and extents must be finite; circle radii must be nonnegative. The framework creates the shape, label and supported control points. Coincident control points prioritize extent handles, allowing zero-radius circles, zero-length lines and collapsed rectangles to expand. The entire label uses inverse scale, keeping text, padding and offset fixed in screen space while its anchor follows image coordinates. Use UpdateGeometry for previews and programmatic updates. Directly changing WPF properties is not a measurement mutation API. GeometryChanged reports the new immutable geometry after model, label and result invalidation have been applied. Use it to write edits back to an application model. A multi-shape tool creates multiple measurements, each with its own identity, completion and removal lifetime; there is no arbitrary visual attachment path. Viewer.MeasurementCompleted and MeasurementRemoved cover every tool. Completion fires once, excludes previews and does not imply query readiness. Removal fires only for a previously completed item. Snapshots include Id, complete Geometry and GeometryVersion. The event's Measurement handle supports updates and disposal from any thread; disposal is idempotent and safe after closure. Queries and retained results MeasurementOptions.Query selects a MeasurementQueryKind: Query Supported geometry Result None (default) All Geometry label; no pixel subscription Pixel Point, crosshair Sample and integer source coordinate LineProfile Line Ordered samples and source coordinates RegionStatistics Rectangle Clipped region and channel statistics Incompatible combinations are rejected before any visual attaches. Pixel queries use floor coordinates and reject points outside the frame. Line profiles clip to the frame; ROI queries and export share PixelRegion.Clip. Empty targets have no result. Use MeasurementQueryKind.Pixel, LineProfile, RegionStatistics or None. Set ShowProfileWindow = true independently to request an owned plot window on completion. Closing that window removes the measurement. This option requires a line-profile query. The built-in line-profile tool enables it; explicit queries default to data only. Geometry compatibility and the window/query combination are validated before attachment. LineMeasurementGeometry.Length provides the geometric length in image pixels without reading a frame. A length-only measurement therefore has no query result. Distance calculation avoids intermediate square overflow and underflow; positive infinity is returned only when the resulting length cannot be represented by a double. IMeasurement.QueryResult is null until successful publication. QueryResultChanged provides an immutable MeasurementQueryResult, or null when a previous result becomes invalid. The result includes measurement ID, geometry version, source FrameInfo, query kind and read-only copies of samples, coordinates or channel statistics. It is safe to retain the result after another frame, editing or removal. Collections never borrow scheduler buffers. Results are a closed class family. Pattern-match MeasurementSampleResult to read Coordinates and Samples: Query is Pixel for one pair or LineProfile for ordered pairs. MeasurementRegionStatisticsResult exposes a non-null clipped Region and Channels. Common MeasurementQueryResult properties contain only provenance and Query, so unrelated payload fields cannot be accidentally read. None produces no result. Labels and plots update before notification. Geometry changes invalidate immediately; query failure, descriptor change, missing targets and expiration clear obsolete results. The scheduler and query protocol remain internal. Ownership and geometry IViewerMeasurements.Measurements exposes the entire measurement layer for visibility, input policy and clearing. Clear cancels the current interaction and removes all measurements, while retaining drawing layers and HUD. Tool registration and EndInteraction likewise manage viewer-wide state, not only resources created by the caller. Within a tool session, use the context's Finish to end that activation without affecting a replacement session. Measurement events carry immutable snapshots alongside a live editable/removable handle; subscribing is therefore not a read-only observation capability. MeasurementStyle belongs to .Measurements. Viewer.MeasurementStyle configures newly created measurements independently for each viewer. Assignment copies and freezes all brushes on the caller's thread before UI dispatch. Existing measurements retain their normal and selected colors. MeasurementOptions.Style overrides the viewer default for a new measurement and is snapshotted on creation. Each measurement owns immutable MeasurementGeometry, a framework-generated primary visual and label, an optional pixel query subscription and its registered resources. Each tool session owns its own unfinished measurements. A preview is already an owned measurement; Complete retains it and enables queries. Cancelling creation disposes unfinished measurements. Visuals attach once and are not replaced on completion. Geometry uses source-image coordinates. A rectangle stores normalized opposite corners. Editing updates the model before the visual, label and optional plot window. Point and line queries use half-open pixel coverage [0, Width) × [0, Height). Line queries floor clipped endpoints to pixel indices, so fractional coordinates in the last row/column remain sampleable. Input direction and endpoint pixels are retained; lines lying on the exclusive right/bottom boundary are outside the image. Every actual geometry change increments IMeasurement.GeometryVersion and clears results. An equal geometry update is a no-op. Geometry kind cannot change after creation. During a rectangle drag, the opposite corner comes from the drag-start snapshot, so crossing it does not change which corner is fixed. Programmatic updates refresh the primary visual, label and editing control points before public notifications. An external update during dragging replaces the drag baseline; subsequent pointer moves use the same control-point index in that new geometry, preserving its fixed anchor. Labels follow geometry immediately, even when queries are slow or fail. ROI statistics and menu export use the same PixelRegion.Clip conversion of the selected item's geometry. The menu freezes the frame lease and region together; subsequent editing does not change an already captured export request. Editing WPF properties directly is not a supported way to change measurements. Deletion, clear, plot-window closure and viewer closure converge on idempotent item disposal: release specialized resources, then remove the label and primary visual even if a resource fails to close. Removing a visual notifies observers after it is removed, making repeated and reentrant removal harmless. Closing the viewer first stops interaction, cancels queries and disposes items, then clears layers and releases its frames. DisposeAsync waits for in-flight queries to release their own leases, including sources that do not immediately honor cancellation. Interaction Starting a valid measurement ends editing; starting valid editing cancels a measurement. Invalid edit requests do not replace the current session. Escape cancels creation or ends editing; edits already applied are retained. Delete ends the selected editing session before disposing its owner. Clear, hiding the measurement layer, disabling its configured hit testing and viewer shutdown cancel active sessions and release mouse capture. Hiding retains completed items. Losing capture finishes the current drag without deleting the item. Capture failure leaves the editing session active without leaving an active drag. Temporary input suppression never changes configured layer hit-testing flags. Restoring input recomputes effective flags for every layer, including layers created while measuring. A hidden measurement layer does not start new tools. Query execution Configure shared query rates with QueryOptions and inspect QueryMetrics; see query scheduling. Subscriptions have distinct lifetimes. Publication requires the same registration, stable measurement identity, geometry version and frame descriptor. Re-registering an object never accepts work from its previous subscription. Geometry changes, invalid regions, cancellation and disposal prevent stale publication. Query and publication failures are isolated per subscriber; failed results remain invalid. The pixel HUD alone opts into a moving-result policy: geometry changes retain the last coordinate/value pair, and completed samples can publish within the same interaction session. Session and descriptor changes still reject old work. Its completion-based 10 Hz cap and 300 ms display retention do not alter other tools' rates or geometry validation. See pixel query contracts. The scheduler tracks the source frame ID of published results. A newer frame with the same descriptor does not by itself reject an in-flight result: it may publish within MaxResultAge. This bounded-age policy prevents starvation when video arrives faster than queries finish. Changed descriptors and expired results are rejected. A result from an unchanged frozen frame remains valid without repeated queries. Threads and disposal Measurement handles dispatch reads, updates and subscriptions to the Viewer STA. Keep callbacks short and never wait there for a worker that calls Viewer APIs. After closure, Dispose and unsubscription remain safe; Id, Origin and IsDisposed remain readable. Other access requires a running Viewer. Cleanup errors from explicit disposal/clear propagate after safe cleanup; shutdown cleanup failures enter DisposeAsync. Notification exceptions are logged and isolated. Custom tools See custom measurement tools for registration, session creation, resource transfer, reentry and failure handling. The profile window plots sample index against pixel value without changing stored samples. Closing it removes its measurement. Rendering details belong to architecture.

docs/en/menus.html.title: Menus | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/menus.html.summary: Menus 简体中文 Add application actions to the context menu. Retain a registration for the feature lifetime; the Viewer borrows your menu object. Register an action The example assumes a live viewer: using var registration = viewer.RegisterMenuItem( new Fizzy.ImageViewer.Menus.MenuItem("Mark ready", () => viewer.HudLabelText = "Ready")); Implement IMenuItem for custom behavior, or use the action helpers. Helpers accept Action or Func<ValueTask>; return asynchronous work so its completion and failure are observed. Visibility and captured targets Menu visibility is determined by IMenuItem.IsVisible, evaluated on each opening. Action-based helpers accept an optional visibility predicate. Use SeparatorMenuItem for separators; the renderer removes leading, repeated and trailing separators. MenuItem and CheckableMenuItem require a nonempty, non-whitespace header and non-null action (and checked-state getter where applicable); constructors reject invalid arguments before registration. Valid headers are preserved as supplied. Built-in interaction actions capture their target when the menu opens. Cancel Measurement only cancels that activation; a replacement activation, including the same tool, is unaffected. Menu registration lifetime RegisterMenuItem(IMenuItem) returns an IDisposable registration handle. Dispose it from any thread to revoke only that registration; disposal is idempotent and safe after viewer closure. Registering the same object twice creates independent registrations. Ignoring the handle keeps the registration alive until the viewer closes. The viewer never disposes the caller-owned menu object itself. Revocation prevents new callbacks from an already open menu and disables its current item; the next opening omits it. An executing action is allowed to finish, including when it revokes itself or the viewer closes. IMenuItem.ExecuteAsync() returns a ValueTask and starts on the viewer STA; no WPF event objects cross this interface. Bindings await completion and log failures. The same menu object cannot execute again while its action is in flight, including after reopening; other actions remain available. Action helpers accept either Action or Func<ValueTask>. Async work that outlives the viewer must own its resources and avoid depending on the viewer dispatcher after it closes. Visibility/check callbacks run on the viewer STA and may change registrations; registrations added while building the menu appear on the next opening. Do not block these callbacks on another thread that is waiting for a viewer operation. Normal menu closure preserves the pending click until input drains. Explicit revocation or viewer shutdown invalidates it immediately. If menu construction fails after freezing a frame, the viewer resumes submissions, removes partial bindings and closes that opening. Header, visibility and check-state failures are logged at the WPF event boundary; they do not escape into the dispatcher. A later opening evaluates registrations again. Viewer shutdown releases registrations, callbacks and WPF menu bindings. Captured image targets Built-in freeze/export actions retain the committed frame, mapping and applicable ROI captured for that opening. Independent leases let accepted work finish after closure; export never switches to a new frame. Custom asynchronous actions must explicitly choose and own targets. Borrowing Viewer does not promise availability after closure. See snapshots.

docs/en/public-api.html.title: Viewer and lifetime | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/public-api.html.summary: Viewer and lifetime 简体中文 Configure a Viewer window and own its shutdown. Viewer is sealed; application adapters compose an instance rather than access its raw WPF window. Getting started has a complete program that waits for user closure. Configure and show await using var viewer = new Fizzy.ImageViewer.Viewer(showWindow: false); viewer.Title = "Inspection"; viewer.HudLabelText = "Ready"; viewer.Show(); // Keep the viewer alive for the owning feature's lifetime. Threads and window lifetime The optional ILogger<Viewer> constructor argument defaults to no logging. Omitting it or passing null uses NullLogger<Viewer>.Instance; pass a logger to integrate with the application logging system. new Viewer() requires no logging setup. Construction shows the window by default. Pass showWindow: false to create a hidden viewer, configure it and subscribe to events before calling Show(). A hidden viewer has a running STA and can accept frames; its owner must await DisposeAsync() even if it is never shown. Application adapters should register their resources before showing, and dispose the viewer if their own initialization fails. Window methods and properties synchronously dispatch to the viewer STA and throw ObjectDisposedException once disposal begins. Show restores a minimized window, shows it and requests activation. Hide hides without clearing frames, drawings or measurements. Minimize changes window state without hiding it. IsVisible follows WPF visibility (a shown minimized window is still visible); IsMinimized is independent. Minimizing an already hidden window does not implicitly show it. DisposeAsync closes the window and waits for owned background work and the STA to stop. Repeated calls observe one completion task and its fixed success or failure result. Resource cleanup failures are reported after all remaining safe cleanup and STA exit; subscriber notification failures are logged and isolated. Closed subscriptions are released when that terminal notification is delivered. Construction validates window bounds before starting the STA. If initialization fails, safe resource cleanup runs on the owning thread and background work is drained before the original exception is rethrown. If cleanup also fails, an aggregate preserves both initialization and cleanup errors. Resources whose safe detachment cannot be established remain isolated rather than being released or reused. Application adapters route user closure (Closed) and explicit adapter disposal to one idempotent cleanup task, release application resources and await the owned viewer's DisposeAsync. Keep measurement subscriptions until window cleanup finishes when the adapter forwards removal notifications. Closed is a window notification, not a substitute for awaiting disposal. There is no separate public Close method. Event callbacks run on the viewer STA; do not block them waiting for shutdown or for work that needs that dispatcher. Frame submission retains its explicit ownership and terminal-result contract: submission after closure consumes the frame and returns Closed, rather than using the window property exception policy. Drawing and HUD handle disposal is idempotent after closure. See frame contracts and drawing contracts. HudLabelText controls the upper-right HUD text. IsPixelInfoEnabled defaults to true and controls bottom-left pixel inspection and its query subscription; the context menu uses the same state. Both properties can be configured before showing the window. EndInteraction() cancels unfinished creation or ends editing, preserving completed measurements and edits already applied. FitToViewport centers the full image and may choose a scale outside the ordinary wheel range of 0.01–100. At such a scale, the wheel permits steps toward that range and rejects steps farther away, so very large or small images remain navigable. Use await SetDisplayRangeAsync(range) to change the requested grayscale mapping and observe rendering failures. DisplayRange reads that request; snapshots retain the last successfully committed mapping. A newer request or closure cancels an outstanding update. Without a current frame the call configures future submissions and completes immediately. See display contracts. Draining work and independent leases Disposal drains admitted submissions through release and public completion, including replacement cleanup on submitting threads and frozen/cancelled drops. A pixel source that ignores cancellation can delay shutdown until its work releases its leases. Programmatic disposal is not blocked by CanUserClose or a cancelling window-closing handler. Cleanup failures from owned query leases and menu pins are retained in the disposal result; ordinary query/provider failures remain query failures. Once disposal begins, frame acquisition, snapshot capture, registration and layer operations reject new work with ObjectDisposedException; submission consumes ownership and returns Closed. Previously acquired leases and snapshots remain independently owned. Viewer does not wait for external leases or reclaim their storage early. Accepted capture/export work with independent dependencies may finish after closure. Borrowing viewer capabilities IViewer aggregates the following interfaces and IAsyncDisposable. Viewer implements all capabilities on the same instance; callers can accept the narrow interface they need. Only the owning host disposes the viewer. Borrowed capabilities share its STA, state and shutdown gate and have no independent disposal contract. Interface Namespace Responsibility IFrameSink .Frames Submit owned frames and await commit/drop results ICommittedFrameSource .Frames Acquire current original-frame leases and observe commits IViewerWindow Root Window visibility, placement, title, close policy and Closed IViewerDisplay .Viewport Fit the image to the viewport and configure display range ISnapshotSource .Snapshots Capture independently owned full-frame or region snapshots IViewerDrawing .Drawing Default Markers layer and drawing helpers IViewerMeasurements .Measurements Measurements layer, tools, interaction, style and events IViewerHud .Hud Screen-space text and pixel inspection visibility IViewerMenu .Menus Revocable menu registration IViewerQueries .Imaging Shared query settings and metrics for measurements and HUD using Fizzy.ImageViewer.Frames; static ValueTask<FrameSubmitResult> PublishAsync(IFrameSink sink, ImageFrame frame, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) => sink.SubmitFrameAsync(frame, cancellationToken: cancellationToken); Submission transfers ownership even when the sink rejects or cancels the frame; alternate implementations and test doubles must release it on every terminal path. Frame readers own their acquired leases. A commit event and a subsequent acquisition are not atomic; use FrameSubmissionOptions.OnCommitted for a specific submission's borrowed lease. Global layer composition belongs only to IViewer.Layers: it can enumerate, create, remove and clear layers across both drawing and measurements. Layers.Items snapshots membership, but its elements remain live mutable handles. IViewerDrawing.Markers and IViewerMeasurements.Measurements expose their respective entire layers; clearing one does not clear the other. A renderer needing a particular layer can accept DrawingLayer; a component updating only an existing drawing can accept DrawingHandle. Layer access includes all content and click handles in that layer, not only the caller's creations. Measurement events include immutable snapshots and a live editable/removable measurement handle. Measurement tool registration and EndInteraction manage the viewer-wide state; a tool session should use its context's Finish to end only itself. Query configuration affects the shared scheduler for measurements and pixel HUD, including other callers. Menu and HUD handles instead operate on their individual registration or text. These interfaces describe normal typed dependencies, not security isolation. The same Viewer implements all capabilities and is the sender of viewer events; casts can recover the complete facade. They do not make drawing independent of WPF. Closed is a window notification; the owner still awaits IViewer.DisposeAsync() for complete shutdown. Related capabilities Measurements: interaction, immutable results and notification order. Custom tools: registration and one-use creation sessions. Menus: registration, target capture and asynchronous execution. Drawing and HUD: layers and individual handles. The API reference lists supported symbols. Internal WPF controls and visual trees are not extension points. See architecture for implementation boundaries and the reviewed API baseline.

docs/en/releasing.html.title: Release SOP | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/releasing.html.summary: Release SOP 简体中文 For maintainers publishing v1.2.0 or later. Older releases are not backfilled. A release is complete only when NuGet payload, /v{version}/ documentation, version index and GitHub Release agree. Never move a published tag or overwrite a package. Documentation updates replace the same version directory. NuGet and Pages are separate services; partial publication is recoverable, not atomic. One-time setup In GitHub Settings → Pages choose GitHub Actions. Set the github-pages environment deployment rules to allow main and release tags; the release job runs on tags. Configure approvals according to repository policy. Configure NuGet Trusted Publishing for owner 0xfizzy, repository Fizzy.ImageViewer, workflow release.yml, and environment github-pages where the policy asks for it. Set repository variable NUGET_USER. No persistent API key is stored. Allow the publishing job contents: write, pages: write, id-token: write. PR validation and audit use read permissions. Protect main, release tags and docs-archive; allow the publishing bot to append archive commits, prohibit force pushes and deletion. Keep the environment's tag policy consistent with the workflow. Create the initially empty archive branch using ./scripts/Initialize-DocumentationArchive.ps1. This explicitly pushes a new branch and must be run by an authorized maintainer. It refuses to replace an existing branch. Review the centralized docs/site.json. For an isolated rehearsal repository, change this configuration and workflow/trust settings there; never send rehearsal packages to the production NuGet ID. Run offline failure gates first. Have another maintainer follow this SOP in the isolated environment, including a deployment failure after package publication. Record commit, workflow run URLs, observed outcomes and unresolved manual checks in a retained release-readiness issue. A local fault fixture is not a real OIDC/Pages exercise. Prepare a release Update the project version, release notes, affected English XML/guides, Chinese translations and examples in one reviewed PR. Versions are SemVer without build metadata; the project version is 1.2.0, its tag and documentation directory are v1.2.0. A prerelease such as 1.3.0-rc.1 does not replace latest stable. npm ci npx playwright install chromium ./scripts/Test-Release.ps1 -Version 1.2.0 node scripts/Test-Browser.mjs ./scripts/Serve-Docs.ps1 Review artifacts/release/validation.json, the transcript, test results, package contents and rendered bilingual pages. Local preparation does not require a tag or a clean checkout and cannot create a publishable bundle. Record interaction checks and required benchmark/consumer validation separately; build success is not physical display, mixed-DPI or device verification. Merge the PR after checks pass. A maintainer explicitly authorizes publication by creating and pushing the tag at the reviewed main commit: git status --short git rev-parse HEAD git tag -a v1.2.0 -m 'release v1.2.0' git push origin v1.2.0 Do not tag until HEAD is the reviewed commit and the checkout is clean. The workflow also checks the project version, tag identity and reachability from origin/main. Automated stages and success criteria Prepare: locked restore, library tests, tool/sample builds, strict docs, fault gates, browser checks and package verification. Pack once; regenerate release API reference from DLL/XML extracted from that exact package. New-ReleaseBundle seals checksums and source identity. Archive: create a draft GitHub Release and upload release-bundle.zip, containing the original nupkg, documentation zip, manifest and validation report. Download and verify before publishing NuGet. Actions artifacts are only temporary transport. NuGet: obtain a short-lived OIDC key, publish or download and verify the existing version. Never use --skip-duplicate. Compare all payload entries except NuGet's added signature. Fixed documentation: restore archived site, merge into docs-archive/v{version}/, commit without force, deploy the entire retained site, and verify every online file. The candidate includes the completed stable-version index, but the successful-deployment marker is recorded only after online verification. Completion: record the successful archive commit. Root/latest select the greatest completed stable SemVer in the same deployment. Publish the GitHub Release only after success. The final workflow step must print PASS and the fixed documentation URL. Inspect the GitHub Release (not draft), NuGet version, language navigation, API/search and version selector. Preserve original bundle assets permanently. Archive and Pages writes share a concurrency group with development deployment. GitHub may replace pending jobs; a cancelled job is never proof of release completion. The daily/manual audit reports retained tags with missing, draft or inconsistent releases. Recovery Prefer the workflow's manual dispatch from main, selecting the existing tag: gh workflow run release.yml --ref main -f tag=v1.2.0 gh run list --workflow release.yml --limit 5 Manual recovery uses the reviewed workflow and scripts from main, while package/source identity remains the original tag. Preparation needs contents: write to see draft Release assets; PR validation remains read-only. If a bundle already exists, the workflow downloads it and does not rebuild. If NuGet already contains the version but no archive is visible, preparation stops. Local diagnosis with access to the Release assets: ./scripts/Resume-Release.ps1 -Tag v1.2.0 ./scripts/Test-PublishedRelease.ps1 -Bundle artifacts/bundle -RequireCompleted ./scripts/Test-ReleaseStatus.ps1 Resume-Release only restores and verifies; the workflow continues publication and deployment with appropriate permissions. Repeated successful runs leave fixed contents unchanged and do not downgrade latest. Asset identity conflicts always stop. Failure Action and expected result Validation before archive No package was published. Fix source and review a new unused release identity; do not move the old tag automatically. Interrupted archive upload Check whether the single bundle asset exists. If present, recover it; otherwise rerun the original successful preparation artifact. Same-name different content is rejected. NuGet request timeout Query/download first. Matching payload means continue; absent/indexing output stays incomplete and can be retried. Existing NuGet version differs Stop; investigate identity conflict and choose a new version. Never delete or overwrite to force success. NuGet succeeds, Pages fails Keep the draft and original assets; dispatch the same tag. No repack is performed. Online file/identity mismatch Do not mark completion. Inspect archive commit and deployment/CDN state, then retry. Latest/index deployment fails Fixed version remains; same-tag recovery republishes the verified index. GitHub completion response lost Inspect actual draft status, then rerun. Actions artifact expired Recover from durable GitHub Release bundle and archive branch. Original bundle missing after package publication Stop and investigate; do not rebuild a replacement pretending to be the original. Network retries are bounded; indexing or CDN delay ends in a visible failure rather than presumed success. The audit performs no writes. Workflow logs and GitHub Actions failure notifications are the incident entrypoint. For an unrecoverable automation defect in tagged scripts, use a reviewed workflow fix and the retained bundle; do not mutate the tag or original Release assets. Pages deployment identifies each build by its documentation archive commit, not the package source commit. Development and fixed-version updates can share source code but contain different sites. Artifact names include the stage, run and attempt to avoid collisions on retries. Online content verification remains required after the deployment API reports success. Optional CUDA package Publish Fizzy.ImageViewer.Cuda separately from the same source tag after the core package is available. On a Windows machine with the CUDA build prerequisites, prepare from the tag's exported source, compile native tests without running hardware, run managed CUDA tests, and seal the original package: ./scripts/New-CudaReleaseBundle.ps1 -Tag v1.2.0 ./scripts/Publish-CudaRelease.ps1 -Stage Archive -Tag v1.2.0 -Bundle artifacts/cuda-release-preparation/bundle gh workflow run release.yml --ref main -f tag=v1.2.0 -f component=cuda Review the preparation transcript, test results and bundle validation before Archive. The separate immutable cuda-release-bundle.zip asset contains the package, native hash, source identity and validation report. It does not replace the core bundle or fixed documentation. The workflow downloads and validates this asset, publishes through the same NuGet Trusted Publishing policy, and compares the downloaded NuGet payload. The policy must authorize the CUDA package ID. Resume with the same dispatch; never rebuild an already published version. Hardware, driver and physical display validation are separate from managed tests and native compilation. Documentation updates without publishing a package A completed release and its original package bundle are required. Updates replace /v{version}/ as a whole; removed pages disappear. Prepare requires a clean checkout, creates an isolated worktree and branch from the currently deployed documentation source, and captures the archive SHA. -Branch selects the new branch name. Source changes are compared against the original tag. ./scripts/Update-Docs.ps1 -Action Prepare -Tag v1.2.0 -Branch docs/v1.2.0-update # Edit guides/translations, navigation, sample C# or XML comments. # Review translations, accept hashes, commit; do not change runtime/build/tooling. ./scripts/Update-Docs.ps1 -Action Check -Tag v1.2.0 # Keep running this script from main; Check automatically selects the prepared source. git -C <prepared-source-directory> push -u origin docs/v1.2.0-update ./scripts/Update-Docs.ps1 -Action Start -Tag v1.2.0 -SourceRef (git -C <prepared-source-directory> rev-parse HEAD) ./scripts/Update-Docs.ps1 -Action Status ./scripts/Update-Docs.ps1 -Action Resume -RunId 123456789 ./scripts/Update-Docs.ps1 -Action Rollback -Tag v1.2.0 -ArchiveCommit <successful-archive-sha> Check requires clean committed source and rejects runtime changes before running trusted main tooling. API reference uses the original package DLL with reviewed XML; samples compile against that package. XML, translations, links and Chromium checks must pass. No update modifies NuGet, tags or original Release assets. Start requires a full source SHA. If Prepare was not used, Start captures the current archive SHA. Under the shared deployment lock, a changed archive baseline rejects the candidate. Development deployment also rejects an obsolete main SHA. Run payloads and hashes are durably committed beneath .publication/runs/<run-id>/ on docs-archive; this internal history is excluded from the public site. The branch retains all original payloads in Git history. Version metadata stores the source commit and file hashes; no revision number is assigned. Build and checks precede one whole-site Pages deployment. Only verified deployments enter .publication/state.json with their successful archive SHA. Failed candidates remain resumable and are never used as the base of an unrelated deployment. Resume reuses the persisted run payload without rebuilding and rejects a candidate superseded by a later successful deployment; obsolete development candidates are also rejected. Rollback restores only the requested version from a known successful archive commit and appends a new commit. It does not rewrite history. A successful old package-release retry cannot undo later documentation updates. Root/latest select the highest completed stable package version. Updating an older version does not change that selection. Online verification checks candidate bytes and entrypoints after the deployment API reports success; failures remain visible in Actions. Run ./scripts/Test-DocumentationUpdate.ps1 for overwrite, deletion, recovery, rollback, stale candidate and XML-only source fixtures. Legacy revision directories are removed when the archive is next assembled. Existing active content moves to the direct version path with corrected identity and selector; old revision URLs return 404 without redirection. Original Release assets remain untouched. For development-only preview, initialize the archive once and dispatch docs.yml on main. No package or release tag is needed. With no stable version, the homepage links to /dev/.

docs/en/snapshots.html.title: Snapshots | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/snapshots.html.summary: Snapshots 简体中文 Capture the committed whole image or a region and save it independently of the Viewer. This exports image pixels, not a viewport screenshot or overlays. Capture and save The snippets assume a live viewer and an output path whose contents may be replaced: using Fizzy.ImageViewer.Snapshots; using var snapshot = await viewer.CaptureSnapshotAsync(SnapshotKind.Display); await snapshot.SaveAsync(path, SnapshotEncoding.Png); See the complete export example. Target and ownership A region must be nonempty and wholly inside the frame. Missing input raises InvalidOperationException. Accepted capture owns the dependencies needed to finish after Viewer closure. Dispose the returned snapshot; AcquirePixels() obtains an independent lease that may outlive both snapshot and Viewer. Its coordinates are region-local; Region and SourceFrame retain original provenance. Pending or failed display-range changes do not affect the captured committed mapping. CaptureSnapshotAsync(Raw|Display) captures the current committed frame at call time and returns independent immutable storage. Raw preserves input values; Display applies the committed display mapping without annotations, HUD or viewport scaling. The overload accepting PixelRegion reads only that region. Snapshots record SourceFrame and region origin. Full snapshots explicitly request the entire region; GPU results are never cached back into source storage. One export read per Viewer executes at a time, with at most one additional capture admitted to wait. Further calls throw InvalidOperationException synchronously before acquiring a frame lease. Accepted captures retain the frame current at the call, including while waiting. Completion, cancellation or failure frees the slot. The ROI save menu pins both frame and integer region before opening the file dialog. Dispose snapshots when finished. A save retains its own lease until completion. Raw capture takes ownership of the independently read CPU region without copying it again. That region's release callback runs when the snapshot's final pixel reference is released, including independent pixel leases retained after snapshot disposal. Capture cleans up a candidate snapshot if another owned resource fails to release before delivery; operation and cleanup failures are preserved together. Encoding, cancellation and failure ImageSnapshot.SaveAsync(path, encoding, token) writes a temporary file in the destination directory and replaces the target only after successful encoding. Cancellation is checked before replacement and between TIFF rows; WPF PNG/JPEG/BMP encoding itself is not interruptible. Display exports support PNG, JPEG, BMP and TIFF. JPEG composites transparency onto black. Raw exports require TIFF and never silently quantize high-bit-depth values. Encoding/cancellation and cleanup failures are preserved together, with the operation failure first. Cleanup can fail after the target was successfully replaced; a failed save task does not by itself prove that the destination is unchanged. The context menu's Save Image As... action selects display PNG/JPEG/BMP or raw TIFF through the file dialog's file type. Save Region Image As... offers the same choices when a completed rectangular measurement is selected. TIFF uses uncompressed Classic TIFF, UINT Gray16 or IEEEFP Gray32Float, top-left orientation, RGB channel order and associated/unassociated alpha tags. Bgr32 padding is omitted. Images exceeding the conservative Classic TIFF size bound are rejected; BigTIFF is not implemented. The context menu allows one save at a time. Independently created snapshot objects may be saved concurrently by application code. Captured snapshots remain usable after closing the viewer. Cancellation does not prove native work stopped; operations retain their dependencies through safe completion. Operation and cleanup failures are preserved together. See menu targets.

docs/en/validation.html.title: Validation | Fizzy.ImageViewer
docs/en/validation.html.summary: Validation 简体中文 Use Windows, PowerShell 7 and the pinned .NET SDK. This repository builds independently; no camera or robot is required. Serialize commands sharing library output. Automated WPF tests use hidden windows and injected boundaries; they do not prove physical display, mixed-DPI, remote-desktop or native GPU behavior.
